lines: Harry Houdini died one hundred years ago this Halloween.
And the way you picture it? Hollywood made that up.
Here's the legend. Houdini is lowered upside down into his Water Torture Cell.
A glass tank full of water, his feet locked in wooden stocks.
The curtain closes. The crowd counts. One minute. Two.
The curtain opens, and the greatest escape artist alive never got out.
Great story. Except it comes from a 1953 movie.
The real Houdini first did that trick in Berlin in 1912, and it was not what killed him.
He didn't die on stage. He died in a hospital bed in Detroit, on October 31st, 1926.
He was fifty two.
And what put him there started nine days earlier, in a Montreal dressing room.
A college student knocked on the door with one very strange question.
What he asked, and what happened next, is part two. Follow so you don't miss it.
Part two. The punches that may have killed Houdini.
October 22nd, 1926. Montreal.
Houdini is lying on a couch backstage, still healing from a broken ankle.
A student named J. Gordon Whitehead asks him: is it true you can take any punch to the stomach?
Houdini says yes.
Whitehead hits him. Hard. Several times.
Before Houdini can brace himself. Witnesses said he winced at every blow.
Two days of constant pain later, a doctor finds acute appendicitis and says: surgery, now.
Houdini refuses. He has a show.
Detroit. A fever of one hundred and four.
He passes out on stage, gets revived, and finishes the performance anyway.
His appendix had burst. Peritonitis. Penicillin wouldn't even be discovered for two more years.
He died on Halloween, age fifty two.
The twist? Doctors still can't agree the punches caused it.
The appendicitis may have been there all along.
For ten Halloweens, his wife Bess held a seance, waiting for their secret code: Rosabelle, believe.
In 1936, she finally blew out the candle.
Next, a brand new myth. Vikings never wore horned helmets. So who invented them? Follow for that one.
